Assert that a data frame is empty

Source: R/expect_empty.R
expect_empty.Rd

A pipeline-friendly validation checkpoint. Express a rule as "the set of violations must be empty", build that set with an ordinary filter(), and pipe it in. Emits a success alert when the data frame has zero rows, otherwise warns or aborts with the number of offending rows and the first few printed as a tibble. To keep all of them, write them to disk with dump (see below).

Usage

expect_empty(
  data,
  success_msg = NULL,
  warn_msg = "The dataset is not empty.",
  abort_msg = NULL,
  log = getOption("expectr.log"),
  dump = getOption("expectr.dump")
)

Arguments

data

A data frame or tibble, a database table (dbplyr, e.g. DuckDB) or an Arrow table or dataset; see Database and Arrow tables.

success_msg

Message shown (and logged) when data is empty. If NULL (default), it is "Check passed: <message>" when warn_msg or abort_msg is given, so the log names every check that ran, and "The dataset is empty." otherwise.

warn_msg

Message shown (and logged) when data is not empty and no abort_msg is set. Default: "The dataset is not empty.".

abort_msg

If provided, cli::cli_abort() is called with this message when data is not empty. If NULL (default), a warning is issued instead.

log

Optional path to a log file. The directory is created automatically. Defaults to getOption("expectr.log").

dump

Optional directory. When the check fails, the offending rows are written there as a timestamped CSV file (UTF-8 with BOM, so Excel reads æøå correctly). Defaults to getOption("expectr.dump").

Value

data invisibly.

Details

The rows are deliberately not kept in the session afterwards: on a population register a failed check can hold millions of rows, and they would stay in memory until the next failure.

Messages are shown literally: braces are not interpolated, so regular expressions such as "^\\d{8}$" are safe to use in a message.

A failed check signals a condition of class expectr_failure (a warning or an error) that carries the offending rows in its violations field. Scheduled pipelines can catch it and keep the rows:

tryCatch(
  expect_empty(bad_rows, abort_msg = "Bad rows"),
  expectr_failure = \(e) saveRDS(e$violations, "bad_rows.rds")
)

Logging and dumping

log appends one line per check to a text file, and dump writes the offending rows to a CSV file in a directory. Both default to a global option, so a script can switch them on once at the top instead of repeating the path in every check:

options(
  expectr.log  = format(Sys.time(), "log/%Y%m%d_%H%M%S_checks.log"),
  expectr.dump = "log/violations"
)

A log line has the form time | symbol | message | rows [| dump file]:

2026-06-11 09:00:03 | ✔ | Check passed: NA ids | 0 rows
2026-06-11 09:00:03 | ! | Negative amounts | 3 rows | log/violations/20260611_090003_Negative_amounts.csv

Database and Arrow tables

Every checkpoint also takes a database table from dbplyr, such as a DuckDB table, and an Arrow table or dataset, and checks it where it lives. The violation set is built as a query, and only its size and the preview rows are fetched into R, so a check on a register too large for memory still works. Arrow data is queried through DuckDB with arrow::to_duckdb(). This needs the dbplyr package, and duckdb for Arrow.

con <- DBI::dbConnect(duckdb::duckdb(), "register.duckdb")

dplyr::tbl(con, "persons") |>
  expect_none(is.na(cpr), abort_msg = "Persons without a cpr") |>
  expect_unique(cpr, year)

A checkpoint returns the table it was given, still unevaluated, so the pipeline continues in the database. On a failure the condition's violations field holds the violation set as a query: collect() it to get the rows. dump fetches and writes all of them. Two things differ from data frames, because a database table has no row order: expect_unique() numbers dupid in the order of the key instead of first appearance, and spells starting on the same day are ordered by their end in expect_no_overlap().

See also

expect_none() to check a condition without leaving the pipeline, expect_unique() for keys, tally_violations() to run many rules at once, flag_duplicates() to inspect duplicates, and view_types() to compare column types.

Examples

# Success: no rows
data.frame() |> expect_empty()
#> ✔ The dataset is empty.

# Warning: unexpected rows
dplyr::filter(ggplot2::mpg, cyl > 6) |>
  expect_empty(warn_msg = "Eight-cylinder cars found")
#> Warning: Eight-cylinder cars found
#> ℹ 70 rows found:
#>     manufacturer model     displ  year   cyl trans drv     cty   hwy fl    class
#>     <chr>        <chr>     <dbl> <int> <int> <chr> <chr> <int> <int> <chr> <chr>
#>   1 audi         a6 quatt…   4.2  2008     8 auto… 4        16    23 p     mids…
#>   2 chevrolet    c1500 su…   5.3  2008     8 auto… r        14    20 r     suv
#>   3 chevrolet    c1500 su…   5.3  2008     8 auto… r        11    15 e     suv
#>   4 chevrolet    c1500 su…   5.3  2008     8 auto… r        14    20 r     suv
#>   5 chevrolet    c1500 su…   5.7  1999     8 auto… r        13    17 r     suv
#>   # ℹ 65 more rows
#> ℹ Set `dump` or `options(expectr.dump = )` to write all rows to a CSV file.

# Abort: treat unexpected rows as a hard error
if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{
dplyr::filter(dplyr::starwars, height < 0) |>
  expect_empty(abort_msg = "Impossible: negative height")
} # }

# With logging, set once for the whole script:
if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{
options(expectr.log = "log/checks.log")

dplyr::starwars |>
  dplyr::filter(name == "Harry Potter") |>
  expect_empty(warn_msg = "Harry Potter rows")
} # }
